historical_timeline.summary: Born in Tokyo (Meiji 5, 3rd month, 25th day, in the lunisolar calendar).
Begins the study of classical poetry at the Haginoya.
Her father dies; she becomes head of the household.
Becomes a pupil of Nakarai Tōsui and begins to write fiction.
Opens a small shop in Shitaya Ryūsenji-chō beside the Yoshiwara; it closes in April 1894.
Moves to Hongō Maruyama-Fukuyama-chō; her major works follow.
Dies of tuberculosis at home in Hongō, at 24.
Her portrait appears on the new 5,000-yen note.

claims.statement: Higuchi Ichiyō, whose given name was Natsu (also written Natsuko), was born in Tokyo on the 25th day of the 3rd month of Meiji 5 in the Japanese lunisolar calendar, which is 2 May 1872 in the Gregorian calendar, in official housing within the grounds of the Tokyo prefectural office in Uchisaiwai-chō (now in Chiyoda).

claims.statement: Japan replaced its lunisolar calendar with the Gregorian calendar at the end of Meiji 5: the 3rd day of the 12th month of Meiji 5 became 1 January 1873 (Meiji 6). Dates before then, including her birth, were recorded in the old calendar.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Explains why her birth date is given in two calendars.

claims.statement: From 1886 she studied classical poetry (waka) at the Haginoya academy of Nakajima Utako.

Her father died of illness in the summer of 1889, when she was 17, leaving debts from a failed business; she became head of the household and took on the support of her mother and younger sister, who did washing and needlework, and the family lived in poverty.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; her mother and sister are given no role in the modern episode.

claims.statement: In 1891 she became a pupil of the novelist Nakarai Tōsui and began to write fiction, choosing to earn her living by writing at a time when this was very hard for a woman; her story Umoregi (1892) brought her into the literary world.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors her modern occupation as a writer.

claims.statement: From July 1893 to April 1894 she ran a small shop selling household goods and cheap sweets in Shitaya Ryūsenji-chō, beside the Yoshiwara pleasure quarter (now in Taitō); the shop closed after about ten months, and her life there became material for Takekurabe.
In May 1894 she moved to Hongō Maruyama-Fukuyama-chō (now Nishikata, Bunkyō).
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the place of the index date.

claims.statement: At Maruyama-Fukuyama-chō she wrote the works that made her name, among them Ōtsugomori (1894), Nigorie (1895), Takekurabe (1895 to 1896) and Jūsan'ya; Nippon.com calls the period 'the miraculous 14 months', and the Nipponica encyclopedia calls the time up to January 1896 'the miraculous year'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern episode's attention to her writing; the two sources measure the period differently.
Anchors the low income in the modern social history.

claims.statement: From the beginning of 1896 her health declined rapidly.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the index date and the presenting illness.

claims.statement: She died of tuberculosis on 23 November 1896 at her home in Hongō, at the age of 24. The National Diet Library gives the cause as lung tuberculosis; the Nipponica encyclopedia gives miliary tuberculosis.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the index date. Tuberculosis is documented; the sources differ on its form (pulmonary or miliary), so the modern pulmonary diagnosis is linked to the documented disease, not to either form.

claims.statement: Her portrait appears on the Bank of Japan 5,000-yen note first issued on 1 November 2004, whose back shows Ogata Kōrin's painting of irises; a new 5,000-yen note with a different portrait was first issued on 3 July 2024.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize and treat pulmonary tuberculosis in a 23-year-old writer in Tokyo with a low income, inside Japan's public health system: seven weeks of cough, fevers, night sweats and weight loss resolved into a diagnosis by chest X-ray, three sputum specimens for acid-fast smear, Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra with rifampin resistance, liquid culture and drug susceptibility testing; HIV, hepatitis and pregnancy testing, baseline liver tests, vision testing before ethambutol, and diabetes screening; airborne precautions and immediate notification to the public health center under the Infectious Diseases Control Law; outpatient care with public funding for a smear-negative patient; the choice of the standard six-month regimen (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for eight weeks, then isoniazid and rifampin for eighteen weeks) because her weight is below the 40 kg needed for the four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen; daily video-observed therapy with pyridoxine; monitoring for liver injury and optic neuropathy; a contact investigation of her household led by the public health center; treatment of moderate malnutrition and help with income; contraception counseling for rifampin interactions; and a paced plan that lets her keep writing. The modern episode is a teaching case, not a claim about her real illness or care.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Higuchi returns three days after her first visit for her results and is seen by Dr. Abernathy-Okoye of infectious diseases today. She brought the second and third sputum specimens, the last collected on waking this morning. Since her first visit she has stayed home, slept in her own room with the window open, and worn a surgical mask in the shared rooms; no one has visited. The cough is unchanged, with a little white sputum and no blood, and she still has evening fevers and night sweats. She is eating a little more since the dietitian's first call. She has not written since her first visit. She is worried about the people she lives with and about the cost of treatment.
